clue.text: Clears area for cricket practice

definitions.meaning: to clear a sum is to make it as profit after costs, which is to net it
the practice pitches enclosed by netting where batsmen train

explanation.surface: A groundsman clears a space so the team can practise.
explanation.definitionFit: Clearing a profit is netting it, and cricketers practise in netted enclosures, so one plural word covers both senses.

clue.text: Sermon about English losing initially in a familiar way

indicators.note: the sermon goes round the other pieces, holding them inside

parts.note: a homily is a short sermon

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word losing is taken

explanation.surface: A preacher's sermon about the English losing, delivered in a cosy, folksy style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' looks like part of the cricket story, but only its first letter is used. 'about' puts E and L inside the sermon word, splitting it after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Homely means plain and familiar, so the adverb from it describes doing something in a homely, familiar manner.

clue.text: Perhaps cricket is popular cult

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
a cult is a small religious sect

explanation.surface: Cricket as a game with a devoted, cult-like following.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps cricket' looks like the sport, but here it is the chirping creature.
explanation.definitionFit: The cricket is a chirping jumping creature, an example of this kind of small six-legged animal.

clue.text: Go up and face bowler here

parts.note: a batsman facing the bowler is in, that is, batting
the crease is the marked line where the batsman stands to face the bowler

explanation.surface: A batsman steps up to face the bowler at the wicket.
explanation.walkthrough: The crease is the line painted on a cricket pitch where the batsman stands.
explanation.definitionFit: To rise or grow larger in amount is to go up, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Field one inside silly mid-on

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step
silly suggests something muddled, so the letters of mid-on are jumbled; it is also a real cricket fielding term

parts.note: a means one, as in a single thing

explanation.surface: A fielder stationed at silly mid-on, close in to the batsman.
explanation.walkthrough: Silly mid-on is a real fielding position close to the batsman, so 'silly' passes as part of the name while it signals the jumble; 'inside' places A among the jumbled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A field of study or activity is a domain, an area of knowledge or influence.

clue.text: Hostility from bowler (perhaps Ellison) initially

parts.note: a bowler is a kind of hat, a hard round felt one

indicators.note: only the first letter of the name Ellison is used

explanation.surface: Fierce aggression from a fast bowler such as Richard Ellison, the England seamer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' marks the bowler as one example of a hat. Richard Ellison was an England bowler of the 1980s.
explanation.definitionFit: Hostility is strong dislike or enmity, which this word names.

clue.text: Does run-out cause a lot of noise?

indicators.note: out signals the letters are dislodged and put in a new order, as in being out of place

explanation.surface: Asks whether a run-out in cricket makes the crowd roar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges DOESRUN; the hyphen in run-out hides it.
explanation.definitionFit: To echo or ring loudly is to fill a place with sound, making a great deal of noise.

clue.text: Facing the bowler this time, always or not at all

parts.note: a batsman facing the bowler is in
now means at this time
ay is an old poetic word meaning always or ever

explanation.surface: A batsman reflects on facing the bowler now, always or never.
explanation.walkthrough: AY (also spelt aye) is an archaic word for always.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for 'by no means' or 'in no respect' is a firm negative, equal to saying not at all.

clue.text: Report of Boatman will get to Sri Lanka, perhaps

indicators.note: a report is something said aloud, so the following words are heard rather than read

parts.note: Boatman is the setter, so his own phrase 'I will' becomes I'll

explanation.surface: The setter announces he is travelling to Sri Lanka.
explanation.walkthrough: Boatman is the setter's pseudonym, so 'Boatman will' is 'I'll'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sri Lanka is an island nation, and an isle is an island, so this is definition by example.

clue.text: Upset, or excite, a run down severely

indicators.note: upset means knocked over or disturbed, so the following letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Something meant to upset or excite a batsman who is running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' rearranges OREXCITEA.
explanation.definitionFit: To criticise someone harshly is to tear into them, a figurative stripping of their skin; to run down is to disparage.

clue.text: Players scored with no-balls

parts.note: the cast is the group of actors in a play
to be scored is to be marked or rated

explanation.surface: Cricketers were judged on how many no-balls they bowled.
explanation.walkthrough: A no-ball is an illegal delivery in cricket; here the phrase is read literally as having no testicles.
explanation.definitionFit: A gelded male has had his testicles removed, leaving him literally without balls.

clue.text: Fielding position in the news?

definitions.meaning: a cricket fielding place square of the batsman on the off side
the letters N, E, W and S are each a direction on the compass

explanation.surface: A cricket fielding position that has made the headlines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'news' is read as N, E, W, S, the four compass directions.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both an off-side cricket fielding position and each of the compass bearings, and NEWS spells out the four of them.

clue.text: Starts to play yorkers later on: now this holds things up

indicators.note: the starts of the following words are their opening letters

explanation.surface: A bowler plans to bowl yorkers later on, and now they hold the batsmen up.
explanation.walkthrough: A yorker is a ball bowled at the batsman's feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall steel tower carries overhead power cables, literally holding them up off the ground.

clue.text: Double curve saw one out with a maiden at midwicket

indicators.note: out signals that one letter is dropped from the word before it

parts.note: a means one, a single thing
a maiden is a girl, here given a girl's name, Anne
read as the middle of wicket, its central pair of letters

explanation.surface: A fielder at midwicket saw one ball go out during a maiden over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes A from SAW to leave SW. Midwicket is a fielding position; here it means the middle letters of wicket. A maiden is also a cricket over with no runs.
explanation.definitionFit: It names an S-shaped bend, as in a pipe or tap, which curves one way and then back the other like a bird's long throat.

clue.text: Fielder caught several balls in a row

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
an over is six consecutive balls bowled by one bowler

explanation.surface: A fielder takes a catch after several balls bowled in succession.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a cricket fielding position on the off side, so the player stationed there is a fielder.

clue.text: According to the law, short leg is a supporter

indicators.note: short means lacking, so a part is cut away

parts.note: legally means according to the law
taken as written

explanation.surface: A legal point: a short leg fielder is a team supporter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' removes LEG from LEGALLY. Short leg is also a fielding position close to the batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A friend who backs you in a dispute or war is a supporter, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Thorpe's boundaries risked losing all, even being abrupt

indicators.note: the boundaries of a word are its outermost letters
dropping every even-placed letter leaves the odd ones

explanation.surface: Graham Thorpe hit boundaries but risked losing it all, being brusque about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boundaries' gives TE, the ends of Thorpe; 'losing all even' keeps the odd letters of risked, RSE. Graham Thorpe was an England batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: Curt and brief in speech, a synonym for abrupt.

clue.text: Renovated pitch put back to accommodate English date

parts.note: pitch is the black sticky substance tar

indicators.note: accommodating means taking something in, so other letters go inside
back means the word put is read in reverse

explanation.surface: A groundsman relays the cricket pitch for an English date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns PUT into TUP, and 'to accommodate' puts ED inside it, giving TEDUP.
explanation.definitionFit: Done up in a showy, gaudy way; the phrase means redecorated or smartened up, often cheaply.

clue.text: Cover with solid pace, injecting velocity to avert century

indicators.note: injecting means putting a new letter into the word
averting the century means the letter for a hundred is turned away and lost

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
V is the physics symbol for velocity

explanation.surface: A fast bowler gives the ball pace and speed to stop a batsman reaching a hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: C in PACE is swapped for V.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay flagstones or asphalt over ground is to give it a hard, firm surface.

clue.text: Guardian etc in revolt over introduction of spinning as part of training

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places the first piece above the next

parts.note: newspapers such as the Guardian are the press
people up in arms are in revolt, so up means rebelling

indicators.note: the introduction of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: The newspapers are up in arms about spin bowlers' training regime.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'over' puts UP above S, the first letter of spinning.
explanation.definitionFit: Lowering and raising the body with the arms is a standard exercise in fitness work, part of a training routine.

clue.text: Forgot to run? Lent a googly

indicators.note: a googly is a deceptive spin delivery that turns the unexpected way, so the letters turn into a new order

explanation.surface: A batsman forgot to run after a deceptive delivery was bowled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'googly' rearranges RUNLENTA. A googly is a leg-spinner's ball that turns the opposite way to the one expected.
explanation.definitionFit: Having put knowledge out of mind is having lost it, the opposite of having learnt it.

clue.text: Wickedly excited yell about boundary

indicators.note: about signals the jumbled letters wrap around another piece
excited means stirred up, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: a boundary in cricket can be a six, written VI in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A spectator shouts wickedly in excitement about a boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: A boundary is a hit worth four or six runs; here it is the six, in Roman numerals. 'excited' jumbles, and 'about' wraps the jumble around the numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting in a wicked or malevolent way is acting sinfully, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Extra: a run made without referring to the score

parts.note: a bye is an extra in cricket, a run scored without the batsman hitting the ball
R is the scoring abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A bye in cricket: a run made without anyone checking the scoreboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'score' is the musical one, not the cricket total.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing music from memory or instinct, rather than reading the written notes, is an idiom for improvising.

clue.text: Review of batsman's role losing most fans in the north

indicators.note: a review looks again and rearranges, so the letters are reworked
losing means the letters of the following words are taken away before rearranging

explanation.surface: A review of a batsman's job that loses most of his supporters.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letters of 'of batsman's role', remove those of 'most fans', and rearrange what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means northern, relating to the north, as in the aurora seen in northern skies.

clue.text: Clue for the l-last to bat

definitions.text: Clue for the l-last to bat

parts.words: Clue for the l-last to bat
parts.note: the last batsman in the order; and L, the end of the word tail, is described by this term, with the stammer echoing it

explanation.surface: A stammering hint for the final batsman in the order.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter L is the final letter of the word tail, so it can be clued as this very term; it also names the last batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: The batsman coming in at the bottom of the order is the last to bat.

clue.text: Unlawfully, get Sri Lanka's opener out for a duck

indicators.note: out means the letter is removed

parts.note: to get unlawfully is to steal

indicators.note: the opener of a name is its first letter, also a cricket pun on the opening batsman

explanation.surface: A Sri Lankan opening batsman dismissed for a duck, unfairly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opener' gives S, which 'out' removes from STEAL. A duck is a batsman's score of nought.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a small freshwater dabbling bird, one kind of duck.

clue.text: Boatman's place: long stop

parts.note: a boatman works on the sea

explanation.surface: The setter's fielding place is long stop.
explanation.walkthrough: Long stop is an old fielding position directly behind the wicketkeeper.
explanation.definitionFit: To close up an opening so nothing passes is to stop it.

clue.text: Caught in time — setback in an area

indicators.note: in means one piece goes inside another
set back means turned around, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: an era is a period of time
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A catch taken just in time, after a setback for the side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setback' turns ERA into ARE, and 'in' puts C inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a unit of land measure, roughly 4,047 square metres, so it is an area.

clue.text: Rescue part of wicket before being dismissed

indicators.note: before puts the first piece ahead of the second

parts.note: a bail is one of the two small crosspieces on top of the stumps
a dismissed batsman is out

explanation.surface: A batsman dislodges a bail before being given out.
explanation.definitionFit: Emergency financial help that saves a failing firm or person is a rescue.

clue.text: Bat in centre of Oval, Dickie Bird once blowing his top

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letters
losing his top means the first letter is gone

parts.note: Dickie Bird was a famous English cricket umpire, now retired

explanation.surface: At the Oval, umpire Dickie Bird once lost his temper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oval is a London cricket ground. 'blowing his top' removes U from UMPIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: The blood-drinking bat of the Americas is named after the undead creature, so the word can denote a bat.
